items.title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
items.summary: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.
items.t: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

items.title: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK
items.summary:
NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions

Vital UK services have been hit by a global Microsoft outage that left hospital staff resorting to paper records and fuelled concerns about an over-reliance on a small number of tech companies.

A day of widespread disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s, with court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they might not be able to rely on digital tickets.

Continue reading...
items.t: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK

items.title: What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines
items.summary: Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines.
items.t: What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines

items.title: She gets 16 pelvic exams a day – so yours don’t hurt
items.summary:
Molly Callahan, a gynecological teaching assistant, helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams

On her busiest days, Molly Callahan, has 16 speculums inserted into her vagina. She works full-time as a gynecological teaching assistant (GTA) – a layperson who helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams before they work with actual patients.

It’s not as unpleasant as you might think. In fact, the point is to help students learn how to do it without causing discomfort. Contrary to common belief, pap smears – tests that screen for cervical cancer – don’t have to be painful.

Continue reading...
items.t: She gets 16 pelvic exams a day – so yours don’t hurt

items.title: Democrats are weighing impeachment of RFK Jr. while courting his supporters
items.summary: When Democrats take over Congress in January, one of their many oversight targets will be Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose overhaul of longstanding vaccine guidance and cuts to medical research over the past two years have drawn fiery criticism. Some high-ranking lawmakers have suggested impeaching him.
items.t: Democrats are weighing impeachment of RFK Jr. while courting his supporters

items.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
items.summary:
He's the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee that oversees health aid and he's just announced he's running for Majority Leader. He spoke to NPR about his foreign aid vision.

items.t: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
items.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

items.title: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
items.summary: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.
items.t: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

items.title: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
items.summary: A major study of nearly 1,900 older adults suggests that stopping statins after age 70 may be relatively safe in the short term for people who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke. However, a higher rate of serious cardiovascular events or death during longer follow-up raises questions about the risks of discontinuing these widely prescribed medications.
items.t: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

In the last decade, strong support for kratom and 7-OH products have kept them federally legal. That's started to change. A crackdown for some highly potent products related to kratom is coming.

items.title: ‘Never thought I’d eat that’: how vegetable prescriptions are helping Britons with diabetes
items.summary:
WellFed participants in Cornwall report better blood sugar levels with help of free veg boxes, cooking and gardening

The participants admitted that throughout their life, their food choices had been far from ideal: egg and chips, hearty roasts, raw fry – a Cornish one-pan dish of bacon, potatoes and onions, often fried in lard and once beloved of miners and fishers.

But here they were, at a community orchard in the harbourside town of St Ives in south-west Cornwall, massaging Swiss chard (to soften the leaves), dicing carrots, adding lentils into a pot to create a low-GI, high-fibre – and tasty – shepherd’s bake.

Continue reading...

items.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
items.summary: Republicans and Democrats in North Dakota worked together to limit what people with diabetes have to pay for insulin, joining a growing bipartisan push across the country to protect patients.
items.t: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients

items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.
items.t: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

items.title: What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year
items.summary: As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself.
items.t: What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year

items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.
items.t: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

items.title: WATCH: Trump administration officials announce PTSD research funding for psychedelic drug ibogaine
items.summary: Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.
items.t: WATCH: Trump administration officials announce PTSD research funding for psychedelic drug ibogaine

items.title: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – as it happened
items.summary:
This blog is now closed

On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it.

She said:

I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work.

The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second.

Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said:

The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch.

He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes.

It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’

I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not…
items.t: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – as it happened

Exclusive: Ron Wyden, citing Guardian report, is launching inquiry into whether health secretary lied about Samoa trip during confirmation hearings

items.title: Time running out for young people to receive meningitis B vaccines in UK
items.summary:
Just 28% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received their first dose in one-off campaign, UKHSA says

The clock is ticking for young people in the UK to receive vaccinations to protect against meningitis B, experts have said, as figures reveal fewer than one in three eligible in a one-off campaign have received their first dose.

Earlier this year, an unprecedented outbreak of meningitis B in Kent and clusters of cases in Dorset and Berkshire caused three deaths, as well as lifelong health consequences among some of those who survived.

items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
items.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.
items.t: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
items.t: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

items.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
items.summary:
Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

Continue reading...
items.t: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles

items.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
items.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.
items.t: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

items.title: Afghan women told to ‘go home’ after de facto ban on male doctors treating them
items.summary:
The unofficial Taliban restriction has forced women into desperate and absurd situations as they seek medical help, according to interviews given to the Guardian and Zan Times

Farida*, 37, woke up in excruciating pain one night with a toothache. Over the next few days, the pain intensified. “My teeth had been ruined for years. My molars on both sides of my mouth were severely damaged. I couldn’t sleep at night and could barely eat.”

Farida and her family had returned from Iran earlier this year to live in Herat, a city in western Afghanistan. Like many migrants forced to return, they have struggled to find work and income. In their straitened circumstances, visiting a doctor has become a luxury but the pain forced Farida to a dental clinic in the Bakrabad area of Herat in early July.

Continue reading...

items.title: Grab the wigs – we’re going to the theatre! We meet the audience superfans going crazy for cosplay
items.summary:
Skeleton suits for Phantom of the Opera, garish wigs for Beetlejuice, a Don’t Tell Mama dress for Cabaret … our critic pulls on her cat ears and leotard to investigate a wild new craze

It’s an hour before curtain-up and the queue outside the theatre is full of green wigs and blue faces, all amid a sea of black and white stripes. It is Halloween night and these theatregoers of all ages, snaking around a corner of the West End, are in themed dress for the musical Beetlejuice, adapted from the 80s film.

In other theatres’ queues you might spot a king from Hamilton, the queens of Six and the wizards of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, all bestowing new meaning to the idea of dressing up for the theatre.

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.
items.t: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.
items.t: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

items.title: Consultant doctors in England call off two-day pay strike
items.summary:
Action on 25 and 26 November suspended to allow for formal negotations with the government

Senior hospital doctors in England have called off the 48-hour strike they intended to hold later this month after the health secretary agreed to negotiations about their grievances.

NHS chiefs, who were worried about how hospitals would cope during the action, welcomed the decision by consultants to “pause” their walkout, which was scheduled for 25 and 26 November.

Continue reading...
items.t: Consultant doctors in England call off two-day pay strike

items.title: Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk | Letters
items.summary:
Cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow, notes Dale Vince of the Green Britain Foundation

You report that scientists say moving even partly from dairy products to vegan alternatives could lead to deficiencies in iodine and other micronutrients if the substitutes are not fortified (Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’, 4 November).

To be clear, cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow. As the paper published in the Lancet Planetary Health explains, iodine is in milk because it is added to cattle feed. The vitamin B12 is there because cobalt is added to the feed so the cow’s gut bacteria can make it. Britain has been doing this for decades. If fortification is the answer, and the paper’s authors say it is, then fortify plant milk. It’s better for us and the planet than cow’s milk.

Continue reading...
items.t: Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk | Letters

items.title: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’
items.summary:
Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say

An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.

Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.

Continue reading...
items.t: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’

items.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
items.summary: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
items.t: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

items.title: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds
items.summary:
Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread

A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, ⁠a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread.

For decades, ​efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.

Continue reading...
items.t: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds

items.title: ‘A tremendous step backwards’: US could lose measles elimination status under RFK Jr’s leadership
items.summary:
Country is in the middle of worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases nationally

The United States could lose its measles elimination status this week, an event likely to cement health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr’s legacy of meddling in vaccine policies amid the worst outbreak of the virus in the US in 35 years.

If the US loses its measles-free status, it would join Canada and several European and Asian nations that had eliminated the disease only for it to return.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘A tremendous step backwards’: US could lose measles elimination status under RFK Jr’s leadership

items.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
items.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.
items.t: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

items.title: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts
items.summary: Ancient manuscripts, including the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, have revealed traces of a deadly sheep virus whose history stretches back more than 3,700 years. Scientists discovered that the virus has remained remarkably unchanged for millennia, turning historic parchment into an unexpected record of ancient disease outbreaks.
items.t: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

items.title: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting
items.summary:
Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment

  • Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England

When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions.

“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”

items.title: Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England
items.summary:
Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds

Poultry and captive birds across England must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu.

The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday, which requires free-ranging birds to be kept within fenced areas.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England

items.title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
items.summary:
Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.

(Image credit: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)
items.t: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak

items.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
items.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.
items.t: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

items.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
items.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.
items.t: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

items.title: Disabled people in England ‘have to wait up to two years for wheelchairs’
items.summary:
Ombudsman’s report says delays have profound consequences and limit users’ ability to lead independent lives

Disabled people are having to wait up to two years to get a wheelchair because of delays involving NHS bodies and private firms that make them.

The situation is revealed in a report by the public service ombudsman for England, Paula Sussex, who said hold-ups were having profound consequences and limiting wheelchair users’ ability to lead independent lives.

Continue reading...
items.t: Disabled people in England ‘have to wait up to two years for wheelchairs’

items.title: People in deprived areas of England more than twice as likely to die early, study shows
items.summary:
Premature death risk also varies according to employment and qualifications, shows analysis ‘laying bare the scale of inequalities’

People living in the most deprived areas of England are more than twice as likely to die prematurely than their more affluent counterparts, according to analysis.

The research, conducted by the Health Foundation, took demographic data from the 2021 census to look at differences in premature mortality rates – defined as any adult who died before their 75th birthday – alongside further data on deaths from March 2021 to December 2023.

Continue reading...
items.t: People in deprived areas of England more than twice as likely to die early, study shows

items.title: The vaccine limbo in the US is worsening the measles outbreak
items.summary:
Earlier doses for children, a focus on unvaccinated adults, a risk strategy based on geography – here’s how a functioning ACIP would address the measles outbreak

The US has announced three deaths associated with measles last week, among them a seven-month-old baby in New York and a postpartum woman in Pennsylvania, underscoring the need for a more aggressive vaccination approach – but US recommendations haven’t changed.

Dismantling the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) made it harder for the US to respond to the measles outbreak, with vaccine recommendations staying the same during a historic rise in cases and deaths, four former advisers say.

Continue reading...
items.t: The vaccine limbo in the US is worsening the measles outbreak

items.title: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
items.summary:

items.t: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling

items.title: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
items.summary: A major review of more than 350 studies suggests that eating less protein could slow aging, improve metabolic health, and potentially extend lifespan, challenging the widespread belief that more protein is always better. Researchers warn that many sedentary adults may be consuming too much protein, while emphasizing that individual needs depend on age and physical activity.
items.t: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

In Pennsylvania, health officials use a quiet vaccination campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been hit hard by the measles outbreak.

items.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
items.summary: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why. Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.
items.t: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

items.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

items.title: How the Nvidia revelations could ripple through the AI industry and global economy
items.summary: Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The economic stakes extend well beyond Nvidia itself. With a market value still exceeding $4 trillion, the company has become a major driver of the stock market and a central force in the AI boom. To discuss the financial impact, Geoff Bennett spoke with Mohamed El-Erian.
items.t: How the Nvidia revelations could ripple through the AI industry and global economy

items.title: How Medicaid affected one California House race
items.summary: A Republican in California's Central Valley fended off challengers for years. But his district had a lot of people on Medicaid, and he lost by a large margin this time.
items.t: How Medicaid affected one California House race

items.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.
items.t: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
items.summary: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

items.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
items.summary: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.
items.t: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
